title: Freedom of expression and information integrity are becoming public-infrastructure conditions for democratic accountability, while platforms and AI reshape who controls discourse
source_unit: UNESCO, World Trends in Freedom of Expression and Media Development: Global Report 2022/2025
geography: Global freedom of expression, journalism, media development, information integrity, digital platforms, AI, and public access to information

denominator.unit: global Freedom of Expression Index trend reported by UNESCO from V-Dem-based analysis

freedom_expression_decline.unit: percent global decline in the Freedom of Expression Index since 2012

information_role.value: information as a public good and information integrity
information_role.unit: two analytical lenses of the World Trends Report

democratic_function.value: public access to information, accountability, human rights, electoral integrity, and informed citizenship

positive_countertrends.value: expanded social-media access, collaborative investigative journalism, subscription models, and legal recognition of community media

observations.method: UNESCO synthesis of global media-development evidence and Freedom of Expression Index analysis based on V-Dem data.
observations.uncertainty: An index trend summarizes dimensions of freedom and information access; it does not establish the same experience for every country, group, journalist, audience, or platform user.
observations.subgroup: Journalists, media organizations, community media, public audiences, youth, vulnerable groups, governments, platforms, and civil-society monitors.
observations.counterinterpretation: Some access, investigative collaboration, subscription, and community-media developments can improve information availability even while aggregate freedom indicators decline.

observations.period: 2022-2025; institutional checks, journalism, and democratic accountability

denominator.unit: global media and rule-of-law institutional frame

institutional_protectors.value: pluralistic legislatures, independent judiciaries, media independence, government transparency, and accountability mechanisms
institutional_protectors.unit: reported safeguards for freedom of expression

reported_pressures.value: weakened governance, hostility toward journalists, digital repression, attacks, and information distortion

journalism_function.value: free, independent, pluralistic, and professional journalism as a cornerstone of democratic life and peace

policy_need.value: international norms, information integrity, trusted information, and public access to information

observations.method: UNESCO report chapter synthesis connecting journalism, rule of law, media independence, public accountability, and information access.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies institutional mechanisms and trends but does not prove that a specific safeguard caused a change in trust, voting, protest, peace, or government accountability.
observations.subgroup: Journalists, courts, legislatures, regulators, media owners, public institutions, political actors, and audiences exposed to public information.
observations.counterinterpretation: Independent journalism and institutional checks can coexist with political contestation or low trust; information availability alone does not guarantee shared facts or collective action.

denominator.unit: global digital-information and journalism technology frame

technology_duality.value: technology both amplifies and constrains freedom of expression

ai_information_risk.value: synthetic or altered content and rapid dissemination disrupt information integrity at scale

platform_power.value: economic and political interests of platform-controlling companies shape the information ecosystem

concentration_risk.value: opaque training, operating costs, algorithmic manipulation, targeted advertising, and moderation-policy abuse can concentrate or distort discourse

observations.method: UNESCO chapter analysis of digital platforms, generative AI, journalism, content creation, information integrity, platform governance, and power concentration.
observations.uncertainty: The chapter is an analytical and policy synthesis; it does not estimate a single causal effect of AI or platforms on persuasion, voting, trust, or journalism employment.
observations.subgroup: Journalists, media workers, platform firms, AI developers, users, advertisers, regulators, and communities affected by synthetic or manipulated information.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI and platforms can lower production costs, expand expression, support journalism, and enable new participation when transparency, accountability, and user agency are strengthened.

observations.period: 2022-2025; safety, gender, climate, and public-information vulnerability

denominator.unit: global journalism and public-information vulnerability frame

journalist_safety.value: journalists and media workers increasingly targeted despite international humanitarian and human-rights protections

digital_repression.value: biometric databases, spyware, AI-driven monitoring, and platform-policy weaponization

gender_and_inclusion.value: progress on gender equality has stalled and women face discrimination and violence

environmental_information.value: press freedom, disinformation, attacks on science, and safety of environmental journalists intersect with the climate crisis

public_effect.value: fragmented public spheres can weaken democratic dialogue and institutional checks

observations.method: UNESCO thematic synthesis across journalism safety, gender, technology, climate, science, and information-as-public-good chapters.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies risks and mechanisms but does not observe every journalist's exposure, every audience's access, or a verified downstream political or social outcome.
observations.subgroup: Women journalists, environmental and science journalists, dissenting voices, vulnerable populations, youth, researchers, media organizations, and public audiences.
observations.counterinterpretation: Safety mechanisms, community media, public-interest funding, digital literacy, and trusted information initiatives can buffer vulnerability and widen participation.

related_sources.claim: UNESCO technology chapter on platforms, AI, information integrity, journalism, and power concentration.
UNESCO rule-of-law chapter on institutional checks, journalist protection, digital repression, and public trust.
UNESCO World Trends Report PDF publication source.

boundary: This record adds an information-as-public-good route linking press freedom, journalism, institutional checks, platforms, AI, information integrity, safety, public access, and democratic accountability. It is not individual media-use, persuasion, voting, trust, journalist respondent, or audience-level data, and it does not establish that the reported global index decline caused any particular political behavior.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official UNESCO global report page and rule-of-law and technology chapter pages were reviewed; index decline, journalism/public-good framing, institutional safeguards, digital and AI mechanisms, safety, gender, climate, and information-integrity claims were cross-checked.
